vote.narrative:
Verdict: Recommend, advance to Charlotte as a front-runner, but eyes open. The rubric puts IFS at 61.4 weighted, and honestly that number is carried by the back office, not the field. Commercial viability (4.1/5) and implementation accountability (3.79/5) are the real strengths here. The capability scores are not. Every single functional capability sits between 2.48 and 3.02 out of 5. That's not a platform that wowed anyone on fit; it's one that didn't fall over on the gates and brings a credible delivery organization. For a 60-OpCo PE rollup, a boring, well-supported, single-tenant ERP-adjacent platform that raises the floor is worth a demo slot.

Why advance. The strongest segments are exactly the ones we care most about under a raise-the-floor strategy: the mid-size low-maturity manual shops that are 44% of the estate, and the small newly-tucked-in sub-$15M OpCos. Both land at 2.76/5. IFS is an asset-and-work-order native platform with a real work-to-cash spine (W2C 2.82, SCL 3.02 are the high-water marks). If the common data model holds up, that's the thing we can actually commonalize across OpCos. Agentic/data-platform future scores 3.48 with only Medium data-control risk, which keeps it inside the tent on openness.

Now the money. Four unmet Musts, and two of them are the same wound: no customer-managed encryption keys (SOX-051 and NFR-22, both GAP). We named CMEK a SOX/security gate. IFS passed the overall Must gate, but going into a SOX-controlled environment across 60 OpCos without Service-Logic-owned key rotation is a real exposure, not a checkbox miss. NFR-21 is the one that hits adoption and cash directly: offline sync not meeting the 60-second / 500-transaction bar means techs in basements, mechanical rooms, and rural sites either wait or work around the app. Every workaround is a line item that never makes it onto the invoice, and that's straight revenue leakage plus billing lag that pushes DSO. INT-028, tenant-level API rate limits, sounds like plumbing until you're running 60 OpCos through one integration layer and one noisy OpCo throttles everyone else's nightly sync.

The soft spot for our fanciest OpCos is real too. Project/job-cost control is 2.74 and the large, sophisticated, project-heavy multi-division segment and Strategic/National Accounts both bottom out at 2.75. IFS has an ERP-grade project heritage on paper, so a 2.74 here is a show-me, not a strength. If PJE and RLC (2.48, the weakest thing on the board) don't come up in the demo, the project-heavy divisions will feel under-served and fight the rollout.

What Charlotte, July 13-16, has to prove or IFS drops:
Prove the mobile offline story live. Load 500 pending transactions on a real device, kill the network, reconnect, and time it. No slideware.
Prove the CMEK gap has a credible path. Either they support Service-Logic-owned key rotation with no app downtime, or they tell us exactly how they compensate, because two GAP musts on the same control is a pattern.
Prove I can get at all my own data. Open export, documented schema, two-way integration on a live endpoint, and show the tenant-level API rate-limit controls that INT-028 says are missing today.
Prove project/job-cost on a real project-heavy scenario: WIP, cost-to-complete, retention, multi-phase billing. Make PJE and RLC earn more than a 2.5.
Prove single-tenant isolation and union/non-union data separation for the diverse estate.
vote.dissent: The honest case against my own vote: I'm advancing a platform whose entire functional profile is mediocre and calling it a front-runner because the sales-and-delivery scores are high. Read the capability table again. Nothing clears 3.02 out of 5. The 61.4 weighted total is propped up by Commercial viability at 4.1 and Implementation certainty at 3.79, which are precisely the categories a polished A-team wins during the chase and where win-it-then-disappear risk lives. Strip those two out and what's left is a field-service tool that scores in the twos across operating fit, project control, and the field itself. We warned ourselves not to over-credit a platform that flatters on delivery while the actual work management is thin, and that's exactly what a 55.1 capability total against a 61.4 weighted total is telling me. Add four unmet Musts, with CMEK failed twice against a hard SOX gate and offline sync failed against the one requirement that governs technician adoption, and a stricter reading says this is a Consider-with-conditions, not a Recommend. If the mid-market plurality is the target, a lighter, field-first FSM that techs actually adopt may raise the floor faster and cheaper than an ERP-heavy platform we'll spend the pilot bending toward CMEK and offline parity. The demo shouldn't be a coronation; it should be IFS earning its way off the twos.

requirement_scores.rationale: IFS claims OOB WO creation from multiple intake channels with auto-populated context, and the proposal explicitly references gated completion (time, materials, scope, signature) as standard — but IoT alert intake and true non-skippable gate enforcement need live demonstration to confirm depth beyond marketing language.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show IoT-triggered WO creation with auto-populated equipment context, and prove gates are truly non-skippable (not just warnings) across all intake channels.

evidence.quote: Supported in base IFS Cloud license.

requirement_scores.rationale: OOB claim for configurable WO types with type-specific fields is credible for an enterprise FSM platform of IFS's maturity, but the proposal doesn't show the specific type-field mapping for HVAC/mechanical archetypes (warranty, inspection, project-linked) so demo validation is needed.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show each WO type (demand/T&M, PM, inspection, warranty, project-linked) with distinct required-field sets configured and enforced, not just a generic type selector.

evidence.quote: Included as part of base license in IFS Cloud.

requirement_scores.rationale: Contact list association is OOB but the actual authorized-caller validation at intake — the thing that prevents billing disputes — requires light configuration via workflows and field rules, which is reasonable but adds delivery risk and needs proof it actually blocks rather than warns.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show the intake workflow actively blocking or flagging an unauthorized caller in real time, not just displaying a contact list for the dispatcher to eyeball.

evidence.quote: Validation of authorized callers during intake will require light configuration via workflows, field rules, or portal access. Configurations preserved through future upgrades.

requirement_scores.rationale: Safety holds are OOB and block dispatch, which is the right behavior; credit holds require light configuration of workflows and status rules — the critical question is whether the configured credit hold is a hard system block or still a soft warning that a determined dispatcher can override, which is exactly the failure mode the RFP is trying to fix.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must prove the configured credit hold is a hard system block on dispatch, not an overridable warning — show a dispatcher attempting to schedule a credit-held account and being stopped cold.

evidence.quote: Safety holds preventing scheduling for work orders are provided OOB in IFS Cloud. Credit holds will require light configuration of workflows and status rules to prevent scheduling of work orders.

requirement_scores.rationale: IFS supports a credit check workflow via its open integration architecture and configurable workflow engine, but D&B integration is not mentioned as a pre-built connector — this is an integration build, not a productized capability, and the delivery burden falls on the implementation team.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo or references must show a live D&B (or equivalent bureau) integration triggering a hold before first dispatch, with evidence of who owns and maintains the integration long-term.

evidence.quote: IFS Cloud supports implementation of a credit check workflow prior to dispatching the first service call through its open integration architecture and configurable workflow engine.

requirement_scores.rationale: Parent-child WO hierarchies with rolled-up billing are a core IFS FSM construct and the OOB claim is credible, but the specific 'master contract with sub-jobs rolled into master single billing' pattern for HVAC service needs to be walked through in the demo to confirm billing roll-up works as described.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show a master contract with multiple sub-jobs, all costs and time rolling into a single master invoice, with correct revenue recognition at the master level.

evidence.quote: Included as part of IFS Cloud base license.

requirement_scores.rationale: Multi-visit WO support with per-visit task tracking is a standard IFS FSM capability and the OOB claim is plausible, but the 10-visit example with individual task-level tracking and aggregate billing needs a live walkthrough to confirm it doesn't degrade into a workaround.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show a single WO with 10 discrete visits, per-visit task completion tracking, and a clean aggregate view for billing — not just multiple WOs linked by a reference field.

evidence.quote: Provided OOB and part of IFS Cloud base license.

requirement_scores.rationale: IFS has genuine project management depth (it's a core differentiator vs. pure-play FSM tools) and the OOB claim for project WOs with different granularity is credible, but the specific 'project dailies for 20+ workers' pattern for large mechanical crews needs demo confirmation.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show a project WO with crew-level daily time entry (20+ workers) contrasted against a standard service WO with individual tech detail, and confirm both feed the same billing engine.

evidence.quote: Supported OOB with base license.

requirement_scores.rationale: Configurable lifecycle stages with required-field gates at each transition is a core IFS workflow engine capability and the OOB claim is credible for an enterprise platform; the 5% signature compliance problem is exactly what gated workflows fix, but the demo must prove gates are non-skippable by dispatchers and techs alike.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show a tech or dispatcher attempting to advance a WO stage without completing required fields (especially signature) and being hard-stopped — not warned.

evidence.quote: Supported as part of IFS Cloud base license.
evidence.source: IFS response to Service Logic ERP Selection RFP 7-2-26.pdf

requirement_scores.rationale: Preventing WO closure without time entry is a straightforward gate and IFS claims it OOB — this is a low-complexity enforcement rule that a mature platform should handle cleanly, but it needs to be confirmed on the mobile app as well as the desktop, since techs close jobs in the field.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show a tech attempting to close a WO on the mobile app without time entry and being blocked — desktop-only enforcement does not solve the field problem.

evidence.quote: IFS Cloud supports prevention of work order closure without time entry OOB with basic IFS Cloud license.

requirement_scores.rationale: The automated status cascade to 'Ready to Bill' on WO completion requires light configuration of workflows and business process automation rather than being fully OOB — this is a reasonable answer but the billing velocity payoff (cutting the 15-30 day lag) depends entirely on how cleanly this configured cascade integrates with the ERP billing trigger, which is unproven.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show the full cascade from WO completion to 'Ready to Bill' status firing automatically, and confirm the ERP billing trigger fires without manual intervention — trace one WO from field close to invoice queue.

evidence.quote: When all tasks on a work order are completed, status can automatically be set to complete using light configuration of workflows and business process automation.

requirement_scores.rationale: Per-OpCo configurable requirement levels (signature Y/N, equipment data Y/N) that can be tightened over time is a legitimate IFS capability given its multi-entity architecture, and this is exactly the right answer for a 60-OpCo rollup where day-one enforcement uniformity would kill adoption — but the demo must show the configuration is truly per-OpCo, not a global toggle.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show two OpCos with different signature and equipment-capture enforcement settings running on the same instance simultaneously, and confirm one can be tightened without touching the other.

evidence.quote: Supported OOB with IFS Cloud basic license.
evidence.source: IFS response to Service Logic ERP Selection RFP 7-2-26.pdf

requirement_scores.rationale: IFS describes profiling and validation as part of its migration process, but 'migration tools and validation rules' across 40 heterogeneous OpCo source systems is a consulting engagement, not an automated platform capability — the word 'automated' in the requirement is doing a lot of work that the answer does not satisfy.

requirement_scores.rationale: 'Partially. requirement_scores.rationale: Azure Backup Vault with encryption in transit and at rest, geo-separate secondary DC, and quarterly restore tests is a solid answer that hits all three sub-requirements; the only gap is whether documented results are formally shared with the customer.

requirement_scores.rationale: Post-migration data quality dashboards and alerting are configurable via IFS reporting or Power BI, which is workable but not a native, purpose-built data quality monitoring module — the 95% threshold alerting requires configuration effort and likely BI tool dependency, adding delivery risk.

requirement_scores.rationale: Multi-company architecture with reusable configuration templates is a real IFS capability and directionally meets the need, but 'guided self-service' provisioning for a non-technical OpCo onboarding team is not evidenced — this reads like a consultant-assisted config clone, not a self-service wizard.

requirement_scores.rationale: Validation rules, referential integrity, mandatory field controls at the application/business logic layer are core ERP table stakes and IFS's answer is specific and credible; this is the right place to enforce data quality — at the point of entry — and it covers required fields, format validation, and integrity checks.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Confirm duplicate-check-on-save is configurable for customer and equipment records specifically, since that is the highest-risk duplication vector in an acquisition rollup.

evidence.quote: all data processed through IFS business logic applies validation rules, referential integrity checks, and mandatory field controls.

requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Confirm HA add-on is included in the proposed price and get contractual RPO/RTO commitments in writing.

requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Confirm whether HA deployment is included in the proposed price or is an add-on; get the HA RPO commitment in writing and validate it covers transactional data specifically.

requirement_scores.rationale: IFS confirms TLS 1.2+ with 1.0/1.1 disabled, but the requirement specifically calls for TLS 1.3 enforcement — that's a stricter bar and IFS does not confirm TLS 1.3 as the enforced standard.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Get explicit confirmation whether TLS 1.3 is enforced or merely supported; if only TLS 1.2 is the floor, assess whether that satisfies Service Logic's security policy.

requirement_scores.rationale: HA option limits planned downtime to ~30 minutes per cycle with most updates non-disruptive, but standard deployment does not guarantee zero-impact maintenance — and HA is an upsell.

evidence.quote: IFS does not provide a contractual SLA for specific sync completion times (e.g., <60 seconds for 500 transactions) as performance depends on payload size, network conditions, and other factors.

requirement_scores.rationale: CMEK is a hard gap — IFS manages the keys in Azure Key Vault and customer-managed keys are not supported; for a PE-backed portfolio with data sovereignty concerns, this is a real risk.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Escalate to Service Logic's CISO and PE sponsor to determine whether IFS-managed keys on Azure are acceptable; if CMEK is a firm requirement, this is near-disqualifying.

requirement_scores.rationale: SCIM 2.0 with Azure AD/Entra ID is supported OOB, but IFS explicitly disclaims ownership of the sub-15-minute deprovisioning SLA, pushing it onto the IdP — which means no contractual guarantee on the security control that matters most for rapid offboarding.

evidence.quote: Deprovisioning latency under 15 minutes is governed by the identity provider's provisioning cycle and configuration rather than a fixed IFS Cloud SLA.

agentic_future.rationale: Salesforce scores well on openness: Data Cloud, MuleSoft, and published APIs give the rollup genuine data portability and the ability to swap or augment AI layers without being held hostage to Agentforce specifically — that's the doctrine passing grade. Agentforce ARR growth and the Field Service voice/maps features are real shipped capability, not vaporware, though the exec summary leans on generic 'customer company' language that doesn't yet prove it understands a 60-OpCo HVAC structure with union/non-union complexity. The remaining risk is that Salesforce's ecosystem depth can tempt a rollup into over-building on proprietary low-code tooling, which quietly recreates lock-in at the configuration layer even when the data layer stays open — that's the thing to probe hard in the demo.

vote.narrative:
Verdict: Shortlist, but on a short leash. Salesforce advances to Charlotte because the platform layer is real and the data-control story is the best in the field (agentic-future 4.3/5, data-control risk Low), not because the requirement fit earned it. Capability score is a soft 45/100 and the weighted total sits at 53.9. This is a credible contender with two holes big enough to sink it if the demo doesn't close them.

Start with what I like. Commercial viability is a 4.02 and implementation certainty a 3.39, so I'm not worried Salesforce disappears or can't staff the job. The Agentforce/Data Cloud openness is genuinely differentiated, and since AI features are close to disposable, the thing that matters is that I can get at all my data. Salesforce clears that bar. For the low-maturity tuck-ins and the residential/white-glove OpCos, this raises the floor, which is exactly the OpCo-diversity play I want.

Now the problems, and they cost money. Project/job-cost control is a 1.85 and W2C is a 2.01 at 25% weight. That is the heart of the work-to-cash engine, and it's the weakest thing here. INV-010, PO's linked to work orders and project cost codes, is a flat GAP. No native PO-to-work-order linkage means job costs get reassembled in a spreadsheet or a bolt-on, which is how project-heavy OpCos leak margin and let billing lag stretch DSO. PJM-043, certified payroll WH-347, is a GAP, and for the prevailing-wage project shops that's not a nice-to-have, it's a compliance stop. RLC at 2.0 drags SOX ITGC (BIR-007) and on-demand user access reviews (BIR-023) to Partial, which corporate will care about even when the local business users don't know to ask. That's the classic split-scoring trap, so I'm not letting the field weights drown out the SOX gap.

The single biggest risk is architecture. ENT-020 and ENT-021 are both GAP: single-tenant dedicated compute/storage/network, and physical isolation with audit evidence. Salesforce is multi-tenant SaaS by design. This isn't a config toggle, it's the deployment model. For a 60-OpCo PE-backed rollup with union/non-union and SOX exposure, that's a gate, not a trade-off. The rubric passed the Must gate on the aggregate, but I'm calling this out plainly: if single-tenant isolation is a true non-negotiable for this deal, Salesforce may be architecturally disqualified regardless of how good the platform is. That is the one thing that could end the conversation.

What Charlotte (July 13-16) has to prove:
- The single-tenancy answer. Show me exactly what isolation Salesforce will contractually commit to and whether it satisfies ENT-020/021, or admit it can't. Everything else is secondary to this.
- Native PO-to-work-order and PO-to-cost-code linkage, live, not on a slide. If it takes an ERP bolt-on or custom objects, show the integration and own the maintenance cost.
- Certified payroll WH-347 end to end for a prevailing-wage job, or a named partner that does it with two-way data flow.
- SOX ITGC audit reporting and scheduled user access reviews as GA features, not roadmap.
- Tech adoption on the mobile app for a mixed-maturity crew. Field won't use what's clunky, and unused features pay nothing.

Met-gate-on-paper does not mean fit. Salesforce earns a demo slot on platform and data. It has to earn the finalist slot on work-to-cash and architecture.
vote.dissent: The honest case against my own vote: I may be shortlisting a platform that already failed the one gate I claim is non-negotiable. ENT-020 single-tenant with dedicated compute is a GAP because Salesforce is multi-tenant by architecture, and that isn't fixable in a demo, it's the product. If I truly treat single-tenancy and data isolation as gates rather than trade-offs, then consistency says I cut Salesforce now instead of spending our people's time flying to Charlotte to watch them explain why co-mingled infrastructure is fine actually. Add a 1.85 on project/job-cost and a 2.01 on W2C at 25% weight, plus GAPs on PO linkage and certified payroll, and what I'm really advancing is a strong CRM/data platform that is weak at the exact work-to-cash spine this selection is supposed to be about. There's a real risk I'm rewarding the shiny Data Cloud/Agentforce story and a high commercial-viability score while giving a pass on the boring plumbing that actually collects the cash. If the single-tenant requirement holds firm, this is a no, and shortlisting it just delays an inevitable cut while lending Salesforce false momentum in the room.

vote.narrative:
Verdict: Shortlist, but on a short leash. ServiceMax comes in at 58.3 weighted, and the commercial and implementation-accountability scores (4.08 and 3.78) are the best thing on the page. This is a real FSM platform with a real HVAC pedigree, not a generic deck. That earns it a seat at the Charlotte table. What it has not earned is trust on the three things that actually gate this rollup.

Start with the architecture. ENT-020, single-tenant with dedicated compute and storage, comes back GAP. ServiceMax is multi-tenant SaaS by design, and we said co-mingled infrastructure is not acceptable. That's not a nitpick for a PE-backed rollup that will churn through diligence and eventual sale; data isolation and clean carve-out are the whole point. Right next to it, NFR-18, load-tested to 3x peak concurrent users, also comes back GAP. Across ~60 OpCos with seasonal HVAC surge, 'trust us it scales' is not an answer. If they can't hand over test results on request, that tells you they don't have them.

Then FIN-001, multi-entity consolidation with automated intercompany eliminations for 40+ entities, is answered via PARTNER. Honestly, that one I half-expect. FSM is not an ERP, and consolidation belongs in the finance stack anyway. It reinforces my standing view: no single platform closes this, you need an ecosystem. But a partner dependency on the money-out end of work-to-cash is a DSO risk if the handoff is fragile. I want to see the seam, not a logo slide.

The capability profile is middling and it leans the wrong way for us. RLC at 2.14, PJE at 2.47, ACQ at 2.48 are the weak spots, and those map straight to dollars. Weak project/job-cost control (7.9 of a 15% category) is billing lag and revenue leakage on exactly the project-heavy divisions that bleed margin when WIP isn't gated to invoice. Weak acquisition/onboarding tooling means every tuck-in is a manual slog, and the whole thesis here is buy-and-integrate fast. The two weakest segments, large project-heavy multi-division (2.65) and small newly-tucked-in sub-$15M (2.67), are the two ends of the barbell this deal has to serve. ServiceMax over-serves the sophisticated middle and leaves the floor unraised.

Data control sits at Medium risk, agentic future 2.76. Not a black box, but not open enough to stop worrying about. I care more about whether I can get at all my own data than about any AI feature they demo.

What Charlotte, July 13-16, has to prove:
1. Single-tenant or credible logical isolation. Show me the deployment topology and where our data physically lives. If it's shared infrastructure with no path to dedicated, that's close to disqualifying regardless of the score.
2. The 3x peak load test. Bring the results or run it. No results, treat NFR-18 as failed, not pending.
3. Full data egress. Prove I can extract 100% of our data, including AI/derived data, on our terms.
4. Work-to-cash orchestration, not just data capture. Walk a project job from dispatch through WIP to invoice and show the gates. Prove it's a workflow engine, not a logbook.
5. The consolidation handoff to the finance partner, end to end, with the intercompany elimination actually running.
6. Multi-overlay config. Show residential white-glove and project-heavy running different processes on one platform without forking the codebase.

Advance them. Make them close the gaps with evidence, not narrative.
vote.dissent: The honest case against my own vote: two of the three unmet Musts are architecture gates, not feature gaps, and I keep saying gates aren't trade-offs. ENT-020 single-tenancy and NFR-18 scale both came back GAP. If I hold every other vendor to the wall on single-tenancy and let ServiceMax through to demos on the strength of a pretty commercial score, I'm doing the exact thing I warn against, letting a familiar HVAC name flatter a prior leader. A 58.3 with a hollow project/job-cost core (2.47) and a multi-tenant foundation may be a vendor we advance out of comfort, then spend three demo days confirming what the scorecard already told us. If they walk into Charlotte and can't move off shared infrastructure, we will have burned a slot that a truly single-tenant contender should have had. The disciplined move might be to make single-tenancy a written pre-demo pass/fail, and cut them now if the answer is no, rather than pay for the trip to hear it in person.

requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Demo must show what the close-readiness dashboard actually looks like in ServiceMax and which ERP it has been proven to feed for a multi-OpCo rollup; get a reference on the handoff workflow.

evidence.quote: ServiceMax can contribute operational close-readiness data (e.g., outstanding WIP, unbilled work orders, pending approvals) to inform the close process...but final confirmation is handed off to the ERP.

requirement_scores.rationale: ASC 842 is explicitly out of scope for ServiceMax — answered PARTNER with no named partner, no integration method, no certification status — which is a non-answer on a Should requirement.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: If ASC 842 matters to Service Logic, vendor must name the specific partner, confirm certification, and show the data handoff from ServiceMax to that tool.

evidence.quote: ASC 842 lease accounting is an ERP or dedicated lease accounting software capability and is not a ServiceMax function.
evidence.source: PTC Response to Service Logic FSM RFP.xlsx

requirement_scores.rationale: ServiceMax is the subledger source, not the reconciliation engine — the matching logic lives in the ERP, so this Must is only half-answered; any OpCo with a weak ERP has a real control gap here.
requirement_scores.evidence_gap: Prove in demo that the data exported from ServiceMax is structured well enough to support automated matching in a named ERP (e.g., NetSuite, Sage); get a reference where this reconciliation is actually running.

evidence.quote: ServiceMax serves as a transactional subledger source...that feeds the ERP, and the data exported is structured to support reconciliation, but the reconciliation control and matching logic itself resides in the ERP.

requirement_scores.rationale: Claimed OOB with configurable data lifecycle and security controls, which is plausible on a Salesforce-based platform, but the response is thin — no version, no specifics on how the 7-year retention policy is enforced or audited.

evidence.source: PTC Response to Service Logic FSM RFP.xlsx

requirement_scores.rationale: Multi-currency is a standard Salesforce platform capability and the OOB claim is credible, but the response gives no detail on exchange rate handling, CAD-specific tax treatment, or how currency is isolated per OpCo.

requirement_scores.rationale: In-app help text and workflow prompts are real, but the vendor explicitly says training guides live in customer-owned portals — so the 'in-application training guide' half of this Must is not fully delivered by ServiceMax.

gating.summary: Passes the Must gate. 15 unmet 'Must' requirement(s) noted as risk. Architecture & scale gate (ARCH-GATE): enterprise scale rated Med (bar: High) — mid-market fit, not an enterprise platform for a 40-80 OpCo rollup.

categories.name: Operating fit
categories.rationale: Blends confidence-adjusted W2C, TPA, ACQ, EVG, RLC, and CXR evidence rather than raw yes/config row counts.
evidence_gaps: Ask for a list of named, production-proven ERP connectors and reference customers running ERP coexistence today, not just API availability.
Ask for a reference customer who executed a rollback on a single OpCo mid-wave without affecting live entities; confirm rollback scope covers data, config, and integrations.
Ask for a reference residential OpCo running 200+ calls/day on BuildOps, or a load-test result; do not accept a marketing claim on a Must throughput requirement.
Ask for a reference where a new entity was provisioned post-go-live without impacting existing OpCos; get actual provisioning timeline data from a recent acquisition onboard.
Ask in demo: what is the largest pricebook tested in production, and what is the load time on a mid-range Android device with 10k+ SKUs?

Ask whether SCIM is on a committed roadmap with a GA date, and what compensating control (e.g., SSO-disable blocking auth) is offered in the interim; validate whether IdP-disable alone satisfies the deprovisioning latency requirement for audit purposes.

vote.narrative:
My vote is Reject, and it lines up with the deterministic rubric. BuildOps is a good mid-market HVAC platform that got walked into an enterprise fight it wasn't built for. Enterprise scale rates Med against a High bar, and for a 40-80 OpCo PE rollup that's a gate, not a trade-off. The weighted total lands at 57.6, capability at 54.7 — that's not a close call dressed up as one.

Here's the why, in operator terms. The strongest segments in the scoring are the small tuck-ins and the low-maturity manual shops — the 44% plurality. That tells you exactly what this tool is: a floor-raiser for simple businesses. The moment you point it at the Strategic/National Accounts and the large project-heavy multi-division OpCos, it sags to 2.58-2.59. Those are the OpCos with the revenue concentration and the complex work-to-cash. You don't buy an enterprise platform that's weakest where the money is.

Now the dollars. FSM-063, no parent-child contract relationships — a school district master with 38 sites can't be modeled cleanly. That's billing chaos and revenue leakage on exactly the accounts that matter most. FSM-051, no templatized field quoting, means slower quote-to-cash and quotes that walk out the door in a tech's head instead of the system. PJM-064 warranty auto-start is a straight GAP on an OOB claim that didn't hold up — you'll eat warranty work you should have billed, or miss the clock entirely. And RLC is the weakest capability at 2.02: no union manpower ratios (FSM-087), no state-specific lien waivers (PJM-044), no bond tracking (PJM-009). For any union or project-heavy OpCo that's DSO bleed and compliance exposure, full stop.

The one that ends the conversation for me is BIR-007, SOX ITGC reporting answered via ROADMAP. This is a PE-backed rollup headed toward an exit or audit. SOX is a corporate must-have the local users don't even know to ask for, which is exactly why we score corporate separately from business. A roadmap promise on SOX is not a delivered capability. Treat it as not-met.

Credit where it's due: implementation certainty scores 3.79 and evidence quality 3.39, so this isn't a vaporware pitch — they answered honestly and the delivery story is credible. Data-control risk is only Medium. If we were buying for the small end of the portfolio alone, this would be a different memo.

What they'd have to prove in Charlotte July 13-16 to reopen this: show single-tenant architecture holding up at enterprise transaction volume across many OpCos, not a demo org with 20 techs. Show parent-child contract hierarchy billing live. Show union ratio enforcement and state lien-waiver generation actually running, not slideware. And give a hard GA date with contract language on SOX ITGC, because roadmap doesn't survive an audit. Absent all four, the verdict stands.
vote.dissent: The honest case against my own Reject: 44% of these OpCos are mid-size low-maturity manual shops, and that's precisely where BuildOps scores best. The doctrine says raise the floor across the low-maturity many, not over-serve the sophisticated few. If the real rollout strategy is to standardize the plurality first and let the handful of large project-heavy divisions run on a heavier ecosystem tool, then an enterprise-scale gate calibrated to the hardest 10% may be the wrong lens. BuildOps also posted the cleanest implementation-certainty and evidence scores in the field (3.79 and 3.39) with only Medium data-control risk — meaning what they promise, they likely deliver, which is worth more than a bigger platform that oversells. The scale rating is Med, not Low; that's a maturity question that 18 months and a proven multi-OpCo reference could move. We might be rejecting the best floor-raiser for the majority because it fails at a ceiling only a few OpCos need. Prove the scale claim wrong at a real willing pilot OpCo before we cut it entirely.

external_research.name: BuildOps
external_research.ownership: Private, VC-backed. $127M Series C (Mar 2025) at $1B valuation (unicorn), led by Meritech; Bond Capital and Schneider Electric's SE Ventures participated; ~$225.8M total funding. Pre-profitability/private.
external_research.analyst: Newer entrant; no Gartner MQ/Market Guide or Peer Insights Customers' Choice placement found - a gap vs. incumbents.
external_research.hvac_fit: High - purpose-built for COMMERCIAL trades (HVAC, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire/life-safety); 'largest commercial trade contractor platform'; veteran-owned.
external_research.enterprise_union: Med - designed for large service contracts and multi-location mgmt; integrates with Sage/Vista/QuickBooks; markets union/prevailing-wage construction payroll. Depth at 60-OpCo/3,500-tech scale UNPROVEN - verify references.
external_research.project_financials: Med-High - project mgmt + on-site invoicing; ERP integrations (Vista/Sage) typically carry AIA/WIP. Native AIA G702/G703 + ASC 606 depth not confirmed - verify.
external_research.agentic_ai: Med - markets an 'AI-driven contractor platform'; investing Series C in API architecture (positive for openness), but agentic toolset less mature than Salesforce/IFS.
external_research.risks: Youngest and smallest; least proven at this buyer's scale; no analyst validation; single-tenant and multi-entity governance need confirmation; higher vendor-stability risk despite strong backing.

agentic_future.rationale: ServiceTitan ships real AI capability with Titan Intelligence and Atlas, but the API terms that explicitly bar customers from using platform data to train or benchmark their own models is a near-disqualifying constraint for a rollup that wants to own its AI destiny — the shipped features are transient, the data lock-in is permanent. The single-tenancy story is also softer than advertised: dedicated DB nodes and node-pool isolation are not a fully separate Kubernetes cluster, so the contractual OOB claim on ENT-023 deserves a hard challenge in the demo. A platform that controls what you can do with your own data is exactly the black-box trap the doctrine flags; no amount of Atlas polish changes that math.

vote.narrative:
My vote: Reject. ServiceTitan is a strong mid-market residential/light-commercial platform being asked to carry a 40-80 OpCo enterprise rollup, and it buckles at the architecture line. The scale gate rated Med against a High bar, and that alone is decisive for me. This is a gate, not a trade-off. A weighted 49.9 and capability 45.7 just confirm what the gate already told us.

The why, in operator terms. The place we bleed money is work-to-cash on the commercial and project side, and that's exactly where ServiceTitan is thinnest. FSM-015 NTE threshold alerts came back ROADMAP. On commercial HVAC, uncontrolled NTE overruns are pure margin leakage. You blow past an authorized amount, the customer disputes, and now you're eating the delta or fighting for it while DSO climbs. Answering a Must with roadmap is not a capability, it's a promise, and I don't pay for promises. QTE-006 configurable quote routing is also ROADMAP, which means quote approval discipline lives outside the system. That's billing lag and revenue you never capture.

The union and project-cost gaps are structural, not cosmetic. FSM-087 union manpower ratios (journeyman:apprentice, foreperson per 10) is a GAP. INV-020 vendor qualification records with expiration alerts is ROADMAP. PJM-044 state-specific lien waivers is a GAP, and PJM-009 bonds tracking is only Partial. For the project-heavy and union OpCos, this is where money and legal exposure live. Miss an AZ preliminary lien window and you can forfeit the right to collect on the job entirely. That's not a feature nitpick, that's a receivable that evaporates. RLC scored 1.53/5 and PJE 1.87/5, the two weakest capability areas, and they map precisely onto our most complex, highest-dollar OpCos. The segment scores say the same thing: large, sophisticated, project-heavy multi-division came in at 2.16, National Accounts at 2.2. The tool is happiest with the mid-size low-maturity manual shops, which is the 44% plurality, so there's a real raise-the-floor argument here. But we're not buying a floor-raiser that caps the ceiling for the OpCos that generate the margin.

Data-control risk rated High on the agentic-future read. For a 60-OpCo rollup where the data is the only thing we can truly commonalize, that's a serious mark against, not a footnote. If I can't get at all of my own data cleanly across every OpCo, the AI conversation is over before it starts.

What would have to be proven in Charlotte July 13-16 to reopen this, and I'm skeptical it can be: show NTE threshold alerts and configurable quote routing as GA, in the product, not on a slide. Demo union manpower-ratio enforcement in the scheduler live. Show state-specific lien waiver generation and bond tracking end to end. Prove single-tenant isolation at 60-OpCo scale with real tenant counts and reference architecture, and prove full two-way data export of everything. Absent GA proof on those, roadmap stays not-met and the reject stands.

One note on what's genuinely good, because it's not nothing: implementation certainty at 3.38 and commercial viability at 3.42 are the best categories in the file, and evidence quality at 3.06 means they didn't drown us in requirements theater. If we were buying for the residential white-glove segment alone, this would be a different conversation.
vote.dissent: The honest case against my own reject: we have a 44% plurality of mid-size, low-maturity manual shops, and ServiceTitan is the strongest fit for exactly that group (2.23/5, edged only by residential at 2.27). Our doctrine is to raise the floor across the low-maturity many, not over-serve the sophisticated few. A platform that gets 26+ manual shops onto real scheduling, mobile, and work-to-cash discipline delivers more aggregate dollar value than one that pleases the handful of project-heavy divisions. The Musts we're failing cluster in union, bonds, liens, and project cost, which are concentrated in a minority of OpCos that could plausibly run on a purpose-built project/ERP overlay while ServiceTitan handles the field-service core. The scale gate is a judgment call rated Med, not a proven failure, and their implementation and commercial scores (3.38, 3.42) are the highest in the set, which lowers deployment risk against a rollup that will live or die on adoption. Before we hard-reject, we should at least let Charlotte test whether a segmented deployment (ServiceTitan for the residential and light-commercial majority, something else for the project-heavy tail) beats forcing one enterprise platform onto sixty diverse OpCos. Killing it on the architecture gate might be trading real, provable adoption wins for a theoretical enterprise-scale purity we can't yet confirm any vendor will actually deliver.

external_research.name: ServiceTitan
external_research.ownership: Public (Nasdaq: TTAN) since Dec 2024; IPO ~$625M, ~$8.9B valuation. FY2025 revenue $771.9M (+26%); FY2026 guide ~$895-905M; approaching non-GAAP op profitability.
external_research.analyst: Dominant in residential/commercial trades software; no current Gartner MQ ranking.
external_research.hvac_fit: High - strong trades footprint (HVAC, plumbing, electrical); historically residential-trades-centric, expanding into commercial/construction.
external_research.enterprise_union: Med - 'Enterprise Hub' centralizes multi-location/franchise mgmt; union/prevailing-wage/certified payroll via Miter partnership (NOT native); multi-legal-entity at 60-OpCo scale to be validated.
external_research.project_financials: Med-High - notably strong for a trades platform: AIA-style G702/G703 pay apps, progress billing, schedule of values, retainage, change-order tracking.
external_research.agentic_ai: Med-High capability (Titan Intelligence 'ti'; Atlas agentic sidekick) BUT API terms explicitly restrict using platform/data to train/benchmark AI - conflicts with customer-built-AI strategy.
external_research.risks: AI/data-use API restrictions; residential/light-commercial roots (large multi-month commercial project depth less proven); payroll partner-dependent (Miter); multi-tenant SaaS vs single-tenant; 60-OpCo consolidation to stress-test.
